quote: Our results show that C. blandus foragers exhibit a strong innate preference for ultraviolet (UV, 365 nm) over blue (450 nm) and green (528 nm) wavelengths.

method: polarized, striped optokinetic drum (stripes at e-vectors 0, 45, 90 and 135 degrees, rotated 12 degrees per second, reversing every minute) with eye movements scored; Control 1 (black-and-white vertically striped drum) and Control 2 (plain linear polarizing filter) also run; each stimulus run once per animal; no statistical test reported; no measurement or matching of intensity between the polarizing stripes reported
conditions: two animals caught by seine net in seagrass beds and mudflats at Dunwich, North Stradbroke Island, Queensland, April 2008; kept in flow-through tanks at Moreton Bay Research Station before testing

source.title: Polarization sensitivity and retinal topography of the striped pyjama squid (Sepioloidea lineolata – Quoy/Gaimard 1832)

quote: This is the first behavioural demonstration of a polarized optokinetic response in any species of cephalopod.

value: orients to polarized light down to a lower threshold between degree of polarization 0.04 and 0.32, possibly as low as 0.11
method: beetles rolling dung balls in a 50 cm circular arena; bearing at the arena edge recorded, then each beetle returned to the centre and rolled a second time, with the heading change analysed against stimuli of different degrees of polarization (artificial UV light from fluorescent bulbs and LEDs through a diffuser-and-polarizer stack 12 cm above the arena, the number of diffusers setting the degree of polarization; unpolarized control)
conditions: beetles collected at Stonehenge game farm, South Africa; field tests under clear skies with the moon 86 to 100% illuminated; sample size not stated in the text returned; the paper prints Escarabaeus satyrus (Boheman, 1860), a generic placement (Escarabaeus Zídek & Pokorný, 2011, used as a genus by Deschodt, Davis and Scholtz), filed here under Scarabaeus satyrus per the desk's name authority

source.authors: Foster JJ, Kirwan JD, el Jundi B, Smolka J, Khaldy L, Baird E, Byrne MJ, Nilsson D-E, Johnsen S, Dacke M
source.title: Orienting to polarized light at night—matching lunar skylight to performance in a nocturnal beetle

where: Abstract; single sentence returned in three consecutive pieces, joined by me
quote: We found that the South African dung beetle Escarabaeus satyrus can orient to polarized light for a range of degrees of polarization … reaching a lower threshold between 0.04 and 0.32, possibly as low as 0.11.
note: The cut clause reads 'similar to that observed in diurnal insects,'. Results (summarised by the fetch tool, not quoted): beetles oriented better than controls at DoLP 0.99 and 0.32; DoLP 0.11 showed some indication of improved orientation that was not significant (W=963, P=0.078); 0.04 was the lowest tested. Nocturnal beetle, not a lab strain. Printed year 2019 (Crossref issued year 2018). Crossref lists only an accepted-manuscript (am) Company of Biologists user licence; the page is the publisher's own free full text and prints the copyright line plus a link to that user licence. value: behavioural colour vision confirmed: fish chose coloured stimuli (blue, green, yellow, orange, red) over grey distractors irrespective of luminance
method: choice among a coloured stimulus and two grey distractors of different brightness; fish first trained to approach and turn over vial caps covered with coloured filters (training criterion above 70% success); Experiment 1 tested 24 fish, of which 18 learnt the task and were analysed (the remaining six were omitted); each colour rests on 2 to 5 fish (blue N=4, green N=5, yellow N=4, orange N=2, red N=3)
conditions: wild fish collected from reefs around Lizard Island and One Tree Island by hand and barrier nets and transported to the island research stations or to aquaria at UQ (the page does not tie each experiment to a site); 7 to 21 cm standard length; sex not stated; Experiments 2 to 4 used 16, 8 and 16 fish

source.title: Colour vision and response bias in a coral reef fish

quote: Behavioural experiments confirmed colour vision over their spectral range; triggerfish were significantly more likely to choose coloured stimuli over grey distractors, irrespective of luminance.
note: Colour list and per-colour statistics from Results, Experiment 1 (blue z=2.15, P=0.03; green z=5.07, P<0.001; yellow z=3.63, P<0.001; orange z=2.61, P=0.01; red z=2.12, P=0.03), returned by the fetch tool in pieces. value: preferential foraging response bias to red and green stimuli over blue and yellow, irrespective of pattern
method: foraging response (first model pecked) to coloured models; Experiment 2 (16 fish, two models of semi-randomly chosen colours per trial, stopped early to record an initial bias): red preferred for first model pecked (z=3.55, d.f.=93, P<0.001), followed by green, yellow and blue; red and green above blue (z>2.76, d.f.=93, P<0.01). Experiment 3 (8 fish, 148 trials): red/green/black pattern chosen over blue/yellow/black (first model pecked z=2.90, N=97, P=0.003); luminance non-significant (P=0.12)
conditions: wild fish collected from reefs around Lizard Island and One Tree Island by hand and barrier nets, Experiment 2 at Lizard Island Research Station in October 2008

source.authors: Cheney KL, Newport C, McClure EC, Marshall NJ
source.title: Colour vision and response bias in a coral reef fish

where: Summary (abstract); sentence returned in two consecutive pieces, joined by me
quote: Triggerfish showed a preferential foraging response bias to red and green stimuli, in contrast to blue and yellow, irrespective of pattern.
note: Contrary figure from Results, Experiment 2: there was no difference between blue and yellow (z=1.13, d.f.=93, P=0.26). The paper also states fish showed a significant preference for red in terms of the first model pecked. Experiment 4 (16 fish, blue and yellow models plain, dotted or striped, 128 trials) found no difference for pattern versus solid (z=-0.23, N=135, P=0.82), pattern type (P=0.58) or blue versus yellow (z=-0.85, N=135, P=0.40). The page gives N=97 for 148 trials (Exp. 3) and N=135 for 128 trials (Exp. 4) without explanation. No red-or-green-versus-yellow test is reported; 'over yellow' rests on the Summary sentence and the rank order. A response bias in foraging, not a measure of discrimination ability. value: escape run to a computer-generated looming stimulus began about 2.4 s after the stimulus started moving, about 1 s before the collision
method: crab in a walking simulator device facing a computer-generated object approaching directly at constant speed (20 cm per s from 70 cm, per the fetch summary); escape run distance, speed and timing recorded
conditions: adult males collected in the rías of San Clemente del Tuyú, Argentina; one trial per crab in Fig. 3 (N=18), N=17 in the Fig. 4 data set; the paper prints the name Chasmagnathus granulatus (Decapoda: Grapsidae), a synonym of the accepted Neohelice granulata (Varunidae)

where: Results, Response threshold; sentence returned in two consecutive pieces, joined by me
quote: Because the response started 2.4 s after the stimulus began to move, the animals responded approximately 1 s before the collision.
note: Abstract: a robust and reliable escape response was elicited in all tested animals, and response timing is consistent among individuals and does not habituate at 3 min stimulus intervals.
